title: Choosing a Riverfront Flood Strategy
description: Compare competing infrastructure arguments that manage the same risk through different mechanisms and tradeoffs.
subject: rla
author: Studo
reviewNotes: Mixed-source Arguments practice reviewed for source comparison, evidence quality, one-best-answer logic, and ER transfer.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares the main strength of each proposal?

options.text: The park offers storage and everyday co-benefits, while the wall offers a defined barrier level for the commercial district.
The park guarantees no future flooding, while the wall only improves recreation.
options.whyWrong: Neither project guarantees no flooding, and recreation is a park benefit.

options.text: Both projects work in exactly the same way and differ only in cost.
options.whyWrong: They manage water through different mechanisms and distribute benefits/risks differently.

options.text: The wall stores more water than the park because it costs less.
options.whyWrong: The wall blocks water rather than storing a stated volume.

explanation.whyCorrect: This comparison identifies the distinct function each source emphasizes without pretending they solve risk in the same way.
explanation.quickTip: Compare arguments on the same decision criteria, but preserve differences in mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which limitation of the flood wall is supported by Source B itself?

options.text: It costs more than the park.
options.whyWrong: The stated construction estimate is lower, though full maintenance costs still matter.

options.text: It cannot protect the commercial district under any flood size.
options.whyWrong: Its consultant gives a design elevation it is intended to block.

options.text: It can shift some water to other locations and depends on gates and pumps.
It provides no physical barrier against river water.
options.whyWrong: A barrier is its central function.

explanation.whyCorrect: The coalition's own source acknowledges transferred-water risk and operational dependencies, making this a strong concession rather than an opponent's invention.
explanation.quickTip: A source that acknowledges a limitation can still argue that the benefit outweighs it.

questions.prompt: Why does the resilience note say the proposals do not answer exactly the same question?

options.text: Only the wall has any limitations.
options.whyWrong: The park also has capacity limits and model uncertainty.

options.text: One proposal is legal and the other is illegal.
Only the park has an engineering estimate.
One proposal manages water partly through storage and broader public-space benefits, while the other prioritizes direct barrier protection for a specific district.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sources optimize different benefits, so a fair comparison requires shared criteria such as flood performance, cost, and effects elsewhere.
explanation.quickTip: Before deciding which argument is stronger, ask whether the sources are valuing the same outcome.

questions.prompt: Which claim would be least justified by the evidence?

options.text: The park could reduce peak levels in the modeled design storm.
options.whyWrong: The hydraulic model estimates a 12-18 cm reduction along a defined stretch.

options.text: The wall is designed to block water up to a specified elevation in the protected district.
options.whyWrong: That is the consultant's stated design goal.

options.text: Either project would eliminate all flood risk for Riverbend.
The wall may require measures to handle rainwater behind the barrier.

explanation.whyCorrect: Every source preserves residual risk, and each proposal has capacity or failure limits.
explanation.quickTip: Be suspicious of eliminate/all/guarantee when the source explicitly describes residual risk.

questions.prompt: Which additional analysis would most improve a fair decision between the two proposals?

options.text: A popularity contest for the project names.
options.whyWrong: Naming preference does not compare flood performance or costs.

options.text: A comparison under several flood sizes that includes lifecycle cost, neighborhood effects, failure scenarios, and the value of non-flood benefits.
Only the initial construction cost, with no maintenance or transferred-risk analysis.
options.whyWrong: Initial cost alone ignores major differences highlighted by the sources.

options.text: A guarantee from either consultant that no model can be wrong.
options.whyWrong: Models carry uncertainty; demanding impossible certainty would not improve the comparison.

explanation.whyCorrect: This uses shared criteria and directly addresses the tradeoffs identified across the three sources.
explanation.quickTip: A fair source comparison needs common decision criteria, not just each side's favorite metric.

options.text: The floodable park is clearly superior because recreation is more important than business protection.
options.whyWrong: The sources do not establish that one value should automatically dominate.

options.text: The flood wall is clearly superior because a lower construction estimate proves lower total cost and risk.
options.whyWrong: Maintenance, pumps, transferred risk, and failure conditions remain relevant.

options.text: The park and wall offer different kinds of risk reduction and tradeoffs; choosing between them requires comparing performance, total cost, impacts beyond the protected area, and residual risk under common scenarios.
Because neither option eliminates all risk, the city should do nothing.
options.whyWrong: Residual risk does not mean risk-reduction measures have no value.

explanation.whyCorrect: This synthesis uses the resilience note to place both arguments under common criteria while preserving their distinct strengths and limits.
explanation.quickTip: When sources advocate different mechanisms, synthesis often means building a shared comparison framework.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate claims, evidence, reasoning, and multiple sources under GED-style conditions.
